content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, Egypt is primarily a symbol of bondage and slavery — specifically the world of sin and oppression from which God delivers His people. The Exodus narrative is treated as the paradigm of salvation, so 'Egypt' becomes shorthand for the old life of enslavement (to sin, to the world, to worldly powers) that believers are redeemed out of, with the Exodus itself typologically foreshadowing redemption in Christ. Leaving Egypt = conversion/deliverance; longing to return to Egypt = backsliding toward the old sinful life or worldliness.","primary_basis":["Exodus 1–14 (the bondage and deliverance narrative)","Exodus 20:2 / Deuteronomy 5:6 ('out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery/bondage')","Deuteronomy 6:12; 7:8 (redemption from the house of slavery)","Numbers 11:4–6; 14:2–4 (longing to return to Egypt as unbelief/backsliding)","Hosea 11:1 ('Out of Egypt I called my son')","Matthew 2:13–15 (Hosea 11:1 applied typologically to Christ)","Hebrews 11:24–27 (Moses refusing the treasures of Egypt, choosing affliction with God's people over the 'pleasures of sin')","Jude 5 (the Lord saved a people out of Egypt)","1 Corinthians 10:1–11 (Exodus events as types/examples for believers)","Revelation 11:8 (the great city 'spiritually called Sodom and Egypt')"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Egypt as a symbol of worldly power and false security — trusting human strength, alliances, or resources instead of God. Prominent in the prophetic literature, where reliance on Egypt for military help represents misplaced trust.","basis":["Isaiah 30:1–3","Isaiah 31:1–3 ('Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help')","Jeremiah 2:18, 36","Ezekiel 29:6–7 (Egypt as a 'staff of reed')","Hosea 7:11"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Egypt as the apostate 'world city' or corrupt religious/political system opposed to God — via Revelation 11:8, where the great city is 'spiritually called Sodom and Egypt,' Egypt joins Sodom and Babylon as an emblem of the God-opposing world order (some interpreters apply this specifically to unfaithful Jerusalem).","basis":["Revelation 11:8"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Egypt as a place of refuge and providential preservation — Abraham, Jacob's family, and the child Jesus all find shelter there; in this strand Egypt is an instrument of God's provision rather than a symbol of evil.","basis":["Genesis 12:10","Genesis 45:5–11; 46:1–4","1 Kings 11:40","Jeremiah 26:21","Matthew 2:13–15"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Egypt as an object of future redemption and inclusion among God's people — the prophetic vision that Egypt itself will be healed, worship the LORD, and be called 'my people,' used to emphasize the universal scope of salvation.","basis":["Isaiah 19:19–25 ('Blessed be Egypt my people')","Psalm 87:4 (Rahab/Egypt among those who know God)"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Egypt read simply as a literal historical nation with no fixed symbolic value, its significance varying entirely by context; some historical-critical interpreters resist any standardized symbolic equation.","basis":["General historical-critical method applied to Exodus and the prophets"],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"Egypt is one of the most stable symbols in Christian interpretive tradition. The bondage/deliverance meaning is dominant across patristic (e.g., Origen's and Gregory of Nyssa's readings of the Exodus as the soul's escape from sin), medieval, Reformation, and modern evangelical usage, and is deeply embedded in hymnody and preaching ('leaving Egypt behind'). The alternative senses (false security, refuge, future redemption) are recognized as genuine biblical strands but are context-specific rather than competing definitions; they qualify rather than displace the primary symbol. Liberation theology also uses Egypt as a symbol of political/economic oppression, an extension of the dominant bondage motif rather than a materially different reading."}
